format: General Training: TRUE/FALSE/NOT GIVEN
passage:
Fixing Things Together: The Repair Café Movement

A  In many households, a broken toaster, a lamp with a faulty switch or a jacket with a damaged zip ends up in the bin, even though the problem might take only a few minutes to fix. Replacing items has become so cheap and convenient that repair skills which were once common have gradually disappeared. Over the past fifteen years, however, a growing movement has set out to reverse this trend, one kettle at a time.

B  The first Repair Café was organised in Amsterdam in 2009 by Martine Postma, a former journalist concerned about the amount of waste produced by modern households. The idea was simple: people would bring broken items to a local venue, where volunteers with practical skills would help them to repair them, free of charge. The event proved so popular that a foundation was set up to support others wishing to start their own, and there are now thousands of Repair Cafés around the world, from small villages to large cities.

C  A typical Repair Café takes place once a month in a community hall, library or church. Visitors register on arrival and describe the fault, and are then directed to a volunteer with the relevant skills, such as electrical repairs, sewing or bicycle maintenance. Crucially, visitors are expected to stay and take part in the repair rather than simply leaving the item and collecting it later. Organisers say this is central to the purpose of the events: the aim is not only to fix objects but to give people the confidence to tackle simple repairs themselves.

D  Not every repair succeeds. Some items cannot be opened without breaking them, and spare parts for certain products are unavailable or too expensive. Volunteers often report that modern electronic devices are harder to fix than older ones, partly because components are glued together rather than screwed. When a repair is impossible, volunteers can at least explain why, and visitors frequently say that understanding the problem makes them think more carefully before buying a replacement.

E  The movement has also had an influence beyond the events themselves. Information collected by volunteers about which products fail and why has been shared with researchers and policymakers. In recent years, a number of governments, as well as the European Union, have introduced 'right to repair' rules requiring manufacturers to make spare parts and repair information available for certain types of products, such as washing machines and refrigerators, for a number of years after sale. Campaigners argue that these rules should be extended to a much wider range of goods.

F  For many volunteers, the social side of Repair Cafés is as important as the practical one. Retired engineers, tailors and electricians find a use for skills that might otherwise be forgotten, while younger visitors learn from them. Many events also offer tea and cake, and conversations often continue long after the repair is finished. As one organiser puts it, 'People come with a broken radio, but they leave having met their neighbours.'

Does the following statement agree with the information given in the passage? Choose TRUE if the statement agrees with the information, FALSE if the statement contradicts the information, or NOT GIVEN if there is no information on this.

Martine Postma had previously worked as a journalist.
explanation: B段落「Martine Postma, a former journalist」。TRUE。

passage:
Fairview Leisure Centre: Swimming Pool Timetable (from 1 March)

A  Lane swimming. Monday to Friday, 6.30–9.00 a.m. and 12.00–2.00 p.m. The pool is divided into slow, medium and fast lanes. Please choose the lane that suits your speed and swim in a clockwise direction.

B  Family fun session. Saturdays and Sundays, 1.00–4.00 p.m. Inflatables and floating toys are available. Children under 8 must be accompanied by an adult in the water at all times, and one adult may supervise no more than two children under 8.

C  Aqua fitness. Tuesdays and Thursdays, 7.00–8.00 p.m. A low-impact workout set to music, suitable for all fitness levels. Places must be booked in advance online or at reception, as numbers are limited to 25.

D  Children's swimming lessons. Weekdays, 4.00–6.00 p.m. Lessons for ages 5 to 12 are grouped by ability rather than age. New pupils will be given a short assessment in the water before being placed in a group. Courses run for 10 weeks and must be paid for in full at the start.

E  Quiet swim. Wednesdays, 8.00–9.30 p.m. An adults-only session with soft lighting and no music, ideal for those who prefer a calmer environment. The sauna is also available during this session at no extra cost.

Please note: the pool is closed for cleaning on the first Monday of every month.

passage:
Kestrel Logistics: Hybrid Working Policy

A  Purpose and scope. This policy explains how employees may combine working from home with working in the office. It applies to all office-based staff who have completed their probationary period. It does not apply to warehouse, driving or reception staff, whose roles require them to be on site.

B  Making a request. Employees who wish to work from home for part of the week should first discuss this with their line manager and then complete the online request form. Managers will normally respond within ten working days. Requests may be refused if the needs of the team or the business cannot be met.

C  Attendance. Hybrid workers are expected to spend a minimum of two days per week in the office. Each team will agree on at least one 'anchor' day when all members attend, to support collaboration and training.

D  Equipment and costs. The company will provide a laptop, a headset and, on request, a monitor. Employees are responsible for ensuring that they have a suitable internet connection and a safe place to work. The company does not contribute to household bills such as heating or electricity.

E  Review. Hybrid arrangements will be reviewed after six months, and at any time if there are concerns about performance. Either the employee or the manager may ask for the arrangement to end, giving four weeks' notice.
